title: Publishing & Contributing to ELT Research

points.h: From Action Research to Formal Study
pts: Genuinely interesting action-research findings (Unit 67) can be developed into more rigorous, generalisable formal research.
This typically requires more systematic data collection, a clearer methodological framework, and often collaboration with academic researchers.
Not every valuable finding needs this step — much value is realised simply through local practice improvement.

v: A completed action-research report or journal (Unit 67)

items: Summarize your action-research finding in two sentences: what you changed and what happened.
Answer four screening questions: Is it useful beyond my class? Was my evidence systematic? Could someone repeat it? Is there published research on it?
Spend twenty minutes searching for published studies on the same question (Unit 81).
List what a formal study would need: a sharper question, a larger sample, a baseline or comparison, a defined instrument and consent.
Decide: ‘keep local’, ‘share at a conference’ or ‘develop into a formal study’. All three are respectable outcomes.
A DIET research cell screens several teachers’ reports together and supports one or two further.
Support: a partner reads your report and asks the four questions aloud.
Challenge: draft a one-page proposal with question, method, sample, timeline and ethics.

blocks.x: A scaling-up note from a Class 7 teacher in Tumakuru (written for this book):

lines: Finding: Letting learners plan stories in Kannada before writing in English produced longer and better-organized English stories.
Surprising or useful beyond my class? Yes; many colleagues ban the home language during writing.
Systematic evidence? Partly. I compared word counts, but only for one class and one term.
Needed: two classes, a comparison, a rubric scored by two raters (Unit 46), and consent.
Decision: Present at the district conference first; then decide with a DIET mentor.

body: Purpose: to show scaling up as a choice, not a ladder. Content: a path from ‘Classroom finding’ forking to ‘Improve my teaching’, ‘Share at conferences’ and ‘Formal study’. Style: calm, map-like. Board version: one line splitting into three arrows with labels.

items: Google Scholar (free) and ERIC (free) for checking existing research.
Zotero (free, open source) to store and cite the studies you find.

blocks.x: A decision sheet in the research journal and a visit to the DIET library.

pts: Several ELT journals specifically welcome practitioner research, distinct from purely academic, theory-driven publications.
These outlets often have a lower barrier to entry than top-tier academic journals, while still offering genuine peer review and credibility.
This is often the most realistic first publishing outlet for a practising teacher's genuine classroom findings.

v: Web access or printed journal guidelines; the UGC-CARE list

items: List four or five possible outlets, from association journals to one international practitioner journal.
For each, note audience, word limit, article types, peer review and fees.
Check each journal against warning signs of predatory publishing (see model language), and check Indian journals against the current UGC-CARE list.
Choose the best match for your finding and note its submission guidelines.
A teacher circle builds a one-page ‘outlet guide’ for its district.
Support: start with teachers’ association newsletters and magazines, which often welcome short classroom reports.
Challenge: compare the author guidelines of a practitioner journal and a research journal.

lines: ELT Journal (Oxford University Press): peer-reviewed, practice-linked articles.
Journal of English Language Teaching (ELTAI, India).

blocks.x: Warning signs of a predatory journal: guaranteed acceptance within days; a fee demanded before review; an unverifiable editorial board; unsolicited emails praising your ‘esteemed work’.

body: Purpose: to show that outlets differ in audience and demand. Content: four outlet types (newsletter, magazine, practitioner journal, research journal) against audience, length and review, with a struck-through ‘pay-and-publish’ column. Style: clean grid. Board version: a four-row table.

items: DOAJ, the Directory of Open Access Journals (free) for checking open-access journals.
UGC-CARE list (free, University Grants Commission) for Indian journals. [VERIFY current status of the list]

blocks.x: Printed copies of journals in the DIET library and a hand-copied outlet table.

pts: Professional conferences offer a lower-stakes, more immediate way to share findings and receive feedback before formal publication.
This connects directly to Unit 67's finding-sharing principle, extended from departmental sharing to the wider professional community.
Conference feedback often meaningfully improves a study before it's submitted for formal publication.

v: A finding; slides or chart paper; a feedback slip

items: Choose a local event first: a cluster meeting, a DIET seminar or a district teachers’ conference.
Structure the talk in five parts: the puzzle, the context, what I did, what I found, what I am unsure about.
Keep to one main finding and show real evidence, such as a learner’s writing (with consent) or a simple chart.
End with two specific questions for the audience, and note every question asked.
Within a week, write a revision note: what will I change in my study or write-up?
Present first as a poster, which allows longer one-to-one conversations, after rehearsing with a peer-observation partner (Unit 68).
Support: co-present with a colleague and divide the five parts.
Challenge: submit an abstract to a national conference after the local talk.

blocks.x: Closing questions that invite useful feedback:

lines: Has anyone tried home-language planning with Classes 9 and 10? Did it help or hinder exam writing?
How could I show that the longer stories were also better, not just longer?

blocks.x: An abstract extract (written for this book):

lines: Over one term, 42 Class 7 learners planned alternate stories in Kannada and English. Stories planned in Kannada were longer and received higher organization scores from two raters. The talk shares the procedure and its limits, and invites discussion on how to study home-language planning more rigorously.

Purpose: to give a memorable talk structure. Content: five stepping stones labelled with the five parts, an audience with question marks on the far bank. Style: friendly. Board version: five boxes joined by arrows.

items: Google Slides or Canva for Education (free for teachers) for slides or a poster.

blocks.x: A chart-paper poster and paper feedback slips.

pts: Partnering with university-based researchers can provide methodological rigour and access to publication that a lone practitioner might lack.
Practitioners bring genuine, ground-level classroom access and questions that many academic researchers value and need.
This is a genuinely reciprocal partnership model, not simply academics using teachers as data sources.

v: Teachers with university or DIET partners

items: Identify a partner: a university department, a Regional Institute of English, a DIET or a teacher-education college.
Before meeting, list what you bring (classroom access, questions, knowledge of learners) and need (methods, literature, analysis).
At the meeting, agree the research question together so that it answers a real classroom need.
Draft a simple agreement: roles, timeline, data ownership, consent procedures, how the school will receive findings, and authorship.
Schedule a feedback meeting in the school when results are available.
A DIET links several schools to one university partner, with a DIET lecturer as coordinator.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Part of a partnership agreement (written for this book):

lines: Research question: How do Class 8 learners use Kannada and English when working in groups on a reading task?
Teacher: selects tasks, collects recordings with consent, keeps a research journal.
University researcher: designs the coding scheme, trains the teacher in transcription, leads the analysis.
Authorship: both named on any publication; the teacher is first author on the practitioner article.
Return of findings: a workshop for the school’s teachers.

body: Purpose: to show partnership as reciprocal. Content: a bridge between a school and a university with ‘questions and access’ flowing one way and ‘methods and literature’ the other. Style: clear. Board version: two buildings joined by two arrows.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared agreement and research log.

blocks.x: A printed, signed agreement kept by both partners.

Consent information for learners and parents should be in a language they understand, often Kannada, Hindi or Urdu rather than English. Follow the partner institution’s ethics procedures and guidance such as BAAL (2021) [VERIFY edition year].

pts: Writing for other teachers demands different priorities — practical applicability, clarity, and relevance — than writing for a purely academic audience.
This connects directly to Unit 54's genre-based writing pedagogy — practitioner research writing is itself a distinct, learnable genre.
Many teachers find this practitioner-focused writing genre more natural and accessible than dense academic prose.

items: Read two short practitioner articles from an outlet you are aiming at.
Mark their moves: context, problem, what the teacher did, evidence, reflection, practical advice.
Compare them with a research article’s moves (introduction, literature, method, results, discussion).
Draft your own, using the genre cycle of Unit 54: deconstruct, construct jointly with a colleague, then write alone.
Write a 400-word blog version first, then expand it.
Support: use the move frame below as a template.
Challenge: write two versions of the same finding, one for a practitioner journal and one for a research journal.

blocks.x: Practitioner moves with model sentences (written for this book):

lines: Context: I teach English to 48 learners in a Kannada-medium government high school in Mandya district.
Problem: My learners could answer comprehension questions but rarely wrote more than three sentences of their own.
Action: For six weeks I let them plan in any language before writing in English.
Evidence: Average story length rose from 38 to 71 words; two colleagues also rated organization higher.
Advice: If you try this, start with a picture story and give planning time in class.

blocks.x: The practitioner genre values clarity, honesty about limits and practical detail. It is not a lesser form of academic writing; it has a different purpose and reader, and genre analysis shows how each research genre is shaped by its community’s expectations (Swales 1990).

body: Purpose: to contrast the moves of practitioner and academic articles. Content: two parallel columns of move blocks, practitioner and academic, with lines linking related moves. Style: tidy diagram. Board version: two lists side by side.

items: Google Docs (free) with comments for collegial feedback.

blocks.x: Photocopied articles, highlighters and a handwritten move frame.

points.h: Peer Review, From the Other Side
pts: Understanding how peer review works — as both a potential author and reviewer — supports more critical reading of published research generally.
This connects directly back to Unit 81's critical-research-reading skill, now extended to genuine participation in the review process itself.
This closes a valuable loop between consuming and contributing to the field's shared knowledge base.

v: A short practitioner article (anonymized draft or published); a review template

items: Read the article once for its main message, then a second time critically, using the questions from Unit 81.
Complete a review template: summary, strengths, main concerns, minor points, recommendation.
Phrase every concern as something the author can act on.
In pairs, compare reviews and discuss disagreements.
Note one change you will make to your own writing.
Colleagues exchange drafts and review each other before any submission, a practice sometimes called ‘friendly review’.
Support: provide a list of review sentence starters.
Challenge: read a journal’s published reviewer guidelines and apply them.

blocks.x: Concerns phrased constructively (written for this book):

lines: Unhelpful: The evidence is weak.
Helpful: The article shows that stories became longer. Could the author add one example of a story before and after, or a rubric score, to show whether quality also changed?
A clear, practically useful account. Recommendation: minor revisions, mainly to show evidence of quality and to acknowledge the small sample.

body: Purpose: to show how reviewing and writing inform each other. Content: an article passing between author’s and reviewer’s desks, comments going one way and a revision returning. Style: simple. Board version: two stick figures and a circular arrow.

items: Google Docs (free) with suggestion mode for anonymized friendly review.

blocks.x: A printed draft with margin comments and a paper review template.

body: As a first-time reviewer, say honestly which parts are outside your expertise, and concentrate on what a teacher judges best: is the procedure clear, and would it work in real classrooms?

pts: Open-access publishing and professional blogging increasingly let practitioner research reach working teachers directly, beyond paywalled academic journals.
This connects to this series' own accessible, practitioner-oriented format and distribution approach.
Wider accessibility increases genuine practical impact, which is often practitioner research's primary intended value.

v: An accepted or completed study; a blog or repository account

items: Check the journal’s copyright policy: may you share a preprint or accepted manuscript?
Write a plain-language summary (300–500 words) with one practical takeaway.
Add a classroom resource you created, such as a rubric.
Publish on a free blog, an association website or an open repository, with a Creative Commons licence.
Consider a Kannada or Hindi version for teachers who prefer it.
Record a five-minute voice note summary for teacher WhatsApp groups.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A blog summary opening (written for this book):

lines: What happens when learners plan their English stories in Kannada? In my Class 7, stories grew longer and better organized. Here is what I did, what I found and a planning sheet you can use tomorrow.
This summary and planning sheet are shared under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Please credit the author.

blocks.x: A paywalled article may reach few teachers in rural schools; a clear summary with a usable resource can reach many.

body: Purpose: to show open sharing as widening reach. Content: a locked journal; beside it the same finding travelling as a blog post, a worksheet and a voice note to staff rooms. Style: bright. Board version: a padlock with arrows fanning out.

items: Blogger or WordPress.com (free plans) for a teacher blog.
Zenodo (free) to deposit a paper or resource with a permanent identifier (DOI).

blocks.x: Photocopied one-page summaries distributed at cluster meetings.

points.h: Why This Matters for the Field
pts: Practitioner contributions keep the field's research genuinely grounded in real classroom practice, not purely theoretical or laboratory-based.
This connects to this entire series' consistent emphasis on evidence-informed, but practically grounded, professional judgement.
A profession where practitioners both consume and contribute to research is a genuinely stronger, more self-correcting one.

v: Chart paper; sticky notes; recent action-research reports

items: In groups, list classroom questions that teachers in your district most want answered.
Sort them: already well answered in the literature; answerable locally through action research; needing a larger, formal study.
For the last group, note possible partners and outlets.
Choose one question for a joint study this year and a conference to share it.
Run the activity with pre-service teachers to present research as part of the job.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Questions from a district workshop (written for this book):

lines: Does reading aloud in the home language before English reading improve comprehension in Class 6?
How do Class 9 learners use phones to practise English outside school?
What feedback on writing do learners actually read and act on?
T: Which of these could only be answered here, in our district?
A: The first one. Our learners speak Kannada, Tulu and Konkani at home. Research from elsewhere cannot tell us what happens with that mix.

blocks.x: When practitioners contribute, research stays grounded in real classrooms, and the field corrects itself more quickly (Borg 2010).

body: Purpose: to show practitioners as users and makers of research. Content: a cycle of ‘Read’, ‘Try’, ‘Investigate’, ‘Share’ and ‘Contribute’ around a growing shared knowledge base. Style: clear. Board version: a circle of five labels.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for collecting questions; Google Sheets (free) for the agenda.

blocks.x: Sticky notes sorted into three columns on chart paper.

body: Take one small finding from your action research and write a 300-word summary using the moves in point 5. Send it to a colleague outside your school with one question: ‘Would this be useful to you, and what would you need to know to try it?’

dek: Unit 91 of 100: for teachers whose action research (Tier III) reveals genuinely valuable findings, a path toward contributing to the field's wider, shared knowledge base.

aims.x: Unit 67 showed how a teacher can investigate a question in their own classroom, and it ended with a caution: most action research does its best work locally, by improving the next lesson. Occasionally, though, an enquiry turns up something colleagues elsewhere would genuinely want to know. This unit sets out the routes from such a finding to a shared contribution: conferences, practitioner journals, university partnerships, open sharing and, eventually, the reviewer’s chair.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: judge whether an action-research finding is worth developing into a more formal study, and what that would involve;
identify suitable practitioner-oriented outlets, including Indian journals and teachers’ associations, and avoid predatory ones;
prepare a short conference presentation that invites useful feedback;
plan a reciprocal partnership with an academic researcher or teacher-education institution;
write a practitioner article that follows the conventions of its genre;
read and write a peer review constructively;
share findings openly while respecting ethics, consent and copyright;
explain why practitioner contributions strengthen the profession as a whole.

why: Why this matters. Unit 67 noted some action research is worth developing further. This poster shows what that further development, and eventual contribution, actually looks like.

background.x: The idea that teachers are researchers, not only consumers of research, has a long history. Lawrence Stenhouse (1975) argued that curriculum development depends on teachers studying their own practice, and Marilyn Cochran-Smith and Susan Lytle (1993) described teacher research as a distinct form of knowledge, ‘from the inside’, rather than a weaker version of university research. In ELT, Anne Burns (2010) made action research accessible to working teachers, and Dick Allwright’s Exploratory Practice proposed a gentler form of enquiry built into normal lessons (Allwright and Hanks 2009).

Simon Borg’s review of teacher research engagement found that, although many language teachers value research, relatively few do it or publish it, and the obstacles are mostly practical: time, confidence, access to literature and support from institutions (Borg 2010). Those obstacles are real in Indian schools and DIETs too. Yet India also has strong teacher networks. The English Language Teachers’ Association of India (ELTAI), the All India Network of English Teachers (AINET) and British Council teacher-research initiatives have given classroom teachers conferences, journals and mentoring, often for their first presentation or article (see Smith and Rebolledo 2018 on the exploratory action research approach used in such schemes).

Policy supports this direction. NEP 2020 calls for teachers to be given autonomy and continuous professional development, and for a culture of research in education, including through the proposed National Research Foundation (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 describes teachers as reflective practitioners who adapt the curriculum to their context (NCERT 2023). One further point matters in a multilingual country: good practitioner research about Kannada-, Urdu- or Tulu-speaking learners fills a gap that research from monolingual English-speaking settings cannot fill.

items: Scaling-up note. A written decision on one action-research finding, with the four screening questions answered.
Outlet guide. A comparison of three suitable outlets, including a check for predatory practices.
Practitioner draft. A short article or conference abstract that follows the practitioner genre and states its limitations honestly.
Review. A constructive peer review of a colleague’s draft, with actionable comments and a recommendation.
Which of your classroom discoveries do you think colleagues elsewhere would genuinely want to know?
What stops you, in practical terms, from presenting or writing, and who could help with each obstacle?
What would a fair partnership with a university researcher look like for you?
How does reviewing someone else’s work change how you read published research?
Where do the teachers you know actually meet research? How could your findings reach them there?
What questions about multilingual learners in your district has no one yet asked?

perm: Before sharing a published article, check the publisher’s self-archiving policy. Learner work may be shared only with consent and without identifying details.

All sample findings, abstracts, agreements, reviews and article extracts are written for this book; the teachers and classes described are fictional. Journal names are given for information only; check current details before submitting. Screenshots of Google Scholar, Zotero, DOAJ, Zenodo, ORCID, blog platforms, Padlet or Canva require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Learner work used in presentations or publications requires consent from learners and parents.
next: Coming next. Unit 92 turns to standardised, large-scale testing, examining the institutions and systems behind exams like IELTS, TOEFL and Cambridge in depth.

terms.def: A short summary of a proposed presentation, submitted to a conference for review, stating the topic, context, methods and main findings or argument.
A standard licence that lets creators share their work while specifying how others may use, adapt and distribute it, such as with attribution or for non-commercial use only.

A form of teacher research that begins with an exploration stage, gathering evidence to understand a classroom issue, before planning any change (Smith and Rebolledo 2018). It has been used in teacher-research schemes in India.
Publication of research so that anyone can read it online free of charge; it widens access for teachers without institutional subscriptions.
The evaluation of a research article by independent experts before publication; it is a key marker of quality when teachers judge research sources.

A publication written mainly for teachers that reports classroom-based work and practical ideas in accessible language, such as ELT Journal or English Teaching Professional, as distinct from a purely academic research journal.
Research that teachers carry out on their own classrooms to understand and improve practice, such as action research or exploratory practice.

A publication that charges authors fees but provides little or no genuine peer review or editorial quality control; teachers submitting or citing research should check a journal’s credentials before trusting it.
A version of a research paper shared publicly before peer review; it may be useful but should be read with caution.

A collaboration between teachers and academic researchers or teacher-education institutions, ideally reciprocal, in which both sides shape the questions and benefit from the findings. A DIET and a group of schools might jointly study a reading programme.
